splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether they can be selected after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be established by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock stops running during the period of absconding.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because there is no statutory authorization for such tolling, and the judiciary lacks power to extend punishment without explicit legislative authority.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim previously presented.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to election rules like ballot-receipt deadlines. The outcome affects whether challenges to voting procedures can be adjudicated before elections or must wait until post-election disputes arise.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office suffers a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when challenging state election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes or alter the competitive landscape.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized concern about election rules does not establish a concrete, particularized injury necessary for Article III standing, particularly in pre-election challenges.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses and creates geographic disparities in sentencing outcomes.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the hierarchy between the rule of lenity and deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in criminal contexts. The Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity takes priority. This split affects how ambiguous sentencing enhancements are resolved.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in criminal or quasi-criminal sentencing contexts, resolving ambiguity in favor of the defendant.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes priority over the rule of lenity when the Commission's commentary reasonably interprets an ambiguous guideline, even in criminal sentencing contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2) can validly expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and other inchoate offenses in the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid interpretation deserving deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether it impermissibly expands the unambiguous guideline text. This affects career-offender designations and significantly impacts sentencing ranges.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a valid, authoritative interpretation of the ambiguous guideline text and that 'controlled substance offense' includes conspiracy and other inchoate offenses under Stinson deference.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond what the text allows, thus deserving no deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule criminalizes substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires a match between state and federal drug schedules. Some circuits hold the Guidelines broadly cover any state drug offense regardless of whether the substance is federally scheduled, while others require the substance to be federally controlled. This split significantly affects career-offender and other enhancement determinations.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the career-offender guideline, and any offense under state law involving a controlled substance qualifies.

positions.label: State offense must involve a federally scheduled substance
positions.summary: Holds that to qualify as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines, the state conviction must involve a substance that is also controlled under federal law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can support compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit (in Crandall) held they cannot even contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while other circuits and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) allow consideration of such changes. The Seventh Circuit held the Commission exceeded its authority in promulgating that policy statement.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of (or as the sole basis for) extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement at U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly impose a sentence upon revocation of supervised release to punish a defendant for the conduct underlying the violation, rather than solely to sanction the breach of trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether revocation sentences for supervised release violations may be based on punishing the new criminal conduct or must be limited to sanctioning the breach of the court's trust. The Sixth Circuit allows express punishment for violation conduct under United States v. Lewis, placing it at the extreme end of a circuit split, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences should address only the breach of trust in the supervisory relationship.

positions.label: Punishment for violation conduct is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants at revocation for the conduct underlying the supervised release violation, not just the breach of trust.

positions.label: Revocation sentences should address only breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of a revocation sentence is to sanction the breach of trust inherent in the violation of supervised release conditions, not to punish the defendant for the underlying conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring claims under Bivens or other civil-rights mechanisms.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for all challenges to confinement, including conditions, or whether civil-rights actions remain available for conditions-of-confinement claims. This split has persisted for over 50 years since Preiser v. Rodriguez left the question open.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for confinement challenges including conditions
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is the exclusive or primary remedy for challenges that are intertwined with conditions of confinement, limiting the availability of civil-rights causes of action.

positions.label: Civil-rights actions available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that civil-rights actions (§ 1983 or Bivens) remain available for prisoners challenging conditions of confinement, with habeas exclusive only for challenges to the fact or duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for an order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is governed by the civil deadline (30 days) or the criminal deadline (14 days) under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (subject to the 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Rule 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal proceeding and subject to the shorter criminal appeal deadline under Rule 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether property appreciation occurring between a Chapter 13 filing and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or belongs to the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a split with other circuits that have reached the opposite conclusion under § 348(f)(1)(A).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), coupled with the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a), means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and purpose under § 348(f)(1)(A) protect good-faith converting debtors by preserving post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation for the debtor rather than the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine, joining the First Circuit's approach. Other circuits have been more restrictive in applying the collateral order doctrine to sealing motions, creating tension over when privacy-related sealing denials are immediately appealable.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is effectively unreviewable on final appeal and involves a value of high order (medical privacy), satisfying the collateral order doctrine requirements.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine because privacy interests can be adequately vindicated through other means, including post-judgment appeal.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Shane Group, Inc. v. Blue Cross Blue Shield

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve unsettled legal questions about how business operators must treat customers and what remedies are available for discrimination claims. The grant suggests a circuit split on the applicable standards, with the Second Circuit's approach being sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied its own framework for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality settings, which the Supreme Court found sufficiently problematic or unsettled to grant certiorari.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Applied different or conflicting standards for evaluating discrimination in business establishments, creating the split that prompted SCOTUS review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
